# Project Overview

RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) provides a genome-wide measurement of gene
expression, allowing genes and biological pathways that differ between
experimental conditions to be identified.

This report presents an end-to-end bulk RNA-seq analysis using public data
from **GSE199679**. The analysis progresses from raw paired-end sequencing
reads through sequencing quality control, alignment, gene quantification,
expression-level quality control, differential expression, functional
enrichment, and biological interpretation.

The comparison includes six biological samples:

| Group | Samples |
|---|---|
| Normal melanocytes (NM) | NM_4, NM_5, NM_6 |
| MP46 | MP46_1, MP46_2, MP46_3 |

The analytical steps were developed and validated individually and then
connected using **Nextflow** for reproducible workflow execution. Docker
provides controlled software environments, and the final results are presented
here using Quarto.

## Analysis Workflow

```text
Paired-end FASTQ
       ↓
FastQC + MultiQC
       ↓
STAR alignment
       ↓
SAMtools + RSeQC
       ↓
featureCounts
       ↓
Count QC + filtering
       ↓
DESeq2
       ↓
PCA + sample correlation
       ↓
Differential expression
       ↓
Gene annotation
       ↓
GO + Reactome enrichment
       ↓
Biological interpretation
```

# Sequencing Quality Control

Raw paired-end FASTQ files were evaluated with **FastQC**, and the individual
reports were combined using **MultiQC 1.35**.

FastQC examines individual sequencing files for potential problems such as
base-quality deterioration, unusual sequence composition, duplication,
adapter contamination, and overrepresented sequences. MultiQC combines these
results across all samples, making systematic and sample-specific patterns
easier to identify before alignment.

## MultiQC Summary

The six RNA-seq samples produced **12 FASTQ files**, corresponding to R1 and R2
reads for each paired-end library. Each FASTQ file contained approximately
**5 million 101-bp reads**.

| QC metric | Observation |
|---|---|
| FASTQ files | 12 |
| Biological samples | 6 |
| Reads per FASTQ | ~5 million |
| Read length | 101 bp |
| Reads flagged as poor quality | None |
| Per-base sequence quality | Passed |
| Per-tile sequence quality | Passed |
| GC content | ~47–53% |
| Duplicate reads | ~35–51% |
| Per-base N content | Passed |
| Adapter content | Passed |
| Overrepresented sequences | Mostly passed; limited warnings observed |
| Sequence-content / length modules | Some warnings or failures observed |

## QC Observation

Overall sequencing quality was suitable for downstream analysis. Per-base
sequence quality passed across the FASTQ files, no reads were reported as poor
quality, and read length and sequencing depth were consistent across the
dataset.

GC content ranged from approximately **47% to 53%**. MP46 libraries tended
toward the lower end of this range, whereas NM libraries tended toward the
higher end. Because this pattern broadly followed the biological groups rather
than appearing as an isolated sample-specific deviation, it was interpreted
together with downstream expression-level QC rather than automatically
considered evidence of contamination.

Sequence duplication ranged from approximately **35% to 51%**. Moderate or
high duplication can occur in RNA-seq because highly expressed transcripts are
sampled repeatedly. PCR amplification or reduced library complexity can also
increase duplication. Duplication was therefore considered together with
alignment performance, gene counts, PCA, and sample-to-sample correlation
rather than being used alone to exclude samples.

Some sequence-content and sequence-length FastQC modules produced warnings or
failures. These flags do not automatically indicate unusable RNA-seq data.
Sequence-composition biases can arise from library preparation, transcript
composition, or other protocol-specific effects and therefore require
interpretation in the context of the complete dataset.

Adapter content passed across the dataset. Low levels of Illumina adapter
signal were detectable toward the ends of some reads, but these levels were
not sufficient to trigger an adapter-content warning or failure. A small
number of overrepresented sequences were also detected and were interpreted
according to their abundance and possible origin rather than automatically
removed.

## QC Conclusion

The combined FastQC and MultiQC assessment supported proceeding to alignment
**without additional adapter or quality trimming**.

This decision was supported by consistently good per-base sequence quality,
the absence of reads flagged as poor quality, passing adapter-content results,
consistent sequencing depth, and the absence of a broad sample-specific
sequencing-quality failure.

FastQC warnings were retained and documented rather than automatically
corrected because warnings can reflect expected characteristics of RNA-seq
libraries. Their significance was subsequently evaluated using independent
downstream QC measures including alignment performance, gene assignment, PCA,
and sample-to-sample expression correlation.

## If QC Is Not as Expected

Unexpected FastQC or MultiQC findings should be investigated before deciding
to modify reads or exclude samples.

| Unexpected finding | Possible reasons | Suggested follow-up |
|---|---|---|
| **Low per-base quality** | Quality deterioration toward read ends, poor sequencing signal, sequencing-run or flow-cell problems | Determine whether poor quality is localized or widespread; consider quality trimming if substantial |
| **Adapter contamination** | Library inserts shorter than the sequencing read length, causing sequencing into adapters | Trim adapters and rerun FastQC/MultiQC |
| **Unexpected GC distribution** | Biological composition, library-preparation bias, contamination, or unusual transcript abundance | Compare biological replicates and groups; investigate isolated or unexplained deviations |
| **High duplication** | Highly expressed transcripts, PCR amplification, low starting RNA, or low library complexity | Interpret with expression and library-complexity results; do not remove RNA-seq reads solely because duplication is high |
| **Overrepresented sequences** | Highly expressed transcripts, rRNA, mitochondrial RNA, adapters, or contamination | Identify the sequences and determine whether they represent expected biology or unwanted sequence |
| **High N content** | Poor sequencing signal or uncertain base calling | Determine whether ambiguous bases are localized or widespread; consider filtering if substantial |
| **Strong R1/R2 difference** | Cycle-specific effects, poorer sequencing quality in one mate, or mate-specific contamination | Compare R1 and R2 modules and determine whether targeted preprocessing is justified |
| **One sample differs strongly** | Library-preparation problem, sequencing failure, contamination, sample mix-up, batch effect, or genuine biological variation | Review raw-read QC together with mapping rate, gene counts, PCA, and sample correlation |
| **Many samples share the same problem** | Library-preparation protocol, sequencing-run effect, systematic contamination, or protocol-specific bias | Determine whether the pattern is expected; investigate systematic technical causes when unexplained |
| **High rRNA content** | Incomplete rRNA depletion or inefficient poly(A) selection | Assess rRNA-associated reads and determine whether usable sequencing depth is substantially affected |

Individual FastQC PASS/WARN/FAIL flags were therefore not treated as automatic
sample acceptance or rejection criteria. QC metrics were considered
collectively, and any trimming, filtering, or sample exclusion would require a
documented technical or biological justification.

# Read Alignment

Following raw-read QC, paired-end reads were aligned to the **GRCh38 human
reference genome** using **STAR**.

Alignment determines where sequencing reads originated in the genome. RNA-seq
requires a splice-aware aligner because many reads span exon-exon junctions
created during RNA splicing.

STAR produced coordinate-sorted BAM files representing the genomic alignments
for each sample.

| Sample | Uniquely mapped reads |
|---|---:|
| NM_4 | 95.20% |
| NM_5 | 95.16% |
| NM_6 | 95.11% |
| MP46_1 | 88.29% |
| MP46_2 | 94.31% |
| MP46_3 | 89.23% |

Unique mapping rates ranged from approximately **88.3% to 95.2%**, supporting
successful alignment across all six samples.

The automated Nextflow workflow **reuses the resulting BAM files** for
downstream processing.

# BAM Processing and Library Strandedness

The coordinate-sorted BAM files were indexed using **SAMtools**, allowing
downstream tools to access genomic regions efficiently.

Library orientation was then assessed using **RSeQC
`infer_experiment.py`**.

RNA-seq libraries may preserve information about the strand from which a
transcript originated. Using the wrong strandedness setting during gene
quantification can assign reads incorrectly and alter gene counts.

The libraries were identified as **reverse-stranded paired-end RNA-seq**.
featureCounts was therefore run using:

```text
-s 2
```

# Gene Quantification

Aligned fragments were assigned to genes using **featureCounts** with the
GENCODE v48 gene annotation.

Alignment determines where reads map, whereas gene quantification determines
how many aligned fragments correspond to each annotated gene. The resulting
raw integer counts provide the input required by DESeq2.

The featureCounts output was processed with Python to remove unnecessary
annotation columns, simplify sample names, maintain consistent sample order,
and create an analysis-ready gene-by-sample count matrix.

The initial matrix contained:

```text
78,894 genes × 6 samples
```

# Low-Expression Filtering

Genes with very little read support provide limited information for
differential-expression testing and increase the number of statistical tests.

Genes were retained when they had:

```text
≥10 counts in at least 3 samples
```

| Filtering stage | Genes |
|---|---:|
| Before filtering | 78,894 |
| Retained | **12,728** |
| Removed | 66,166 |

The remaining **12,728 genes** were used for differential-expression analysis.

# Expression-Level Quality Control

Raw-read QC determines whether the sequencing reads are technically suitable
for analysis. After gene quantification, expression-level QC provides another
independent assessment of sample relationships and biological replicate
consistency.

DESeq2 **variance-stabilizing transformation (VST)** was used to generate
expression values suitable for PCA and sample-correlation analysis.

## Principal Component Analysis

Principal component analysis summarizes major sources of expression variation
across thousands of genes.

![](images/pca_expression_qc.png){fig-alt="PCA showing separation between NM and MP46 samples" width=80%}

The first two principal components explained:

```text
PC1 = 88.79%
PC2 =  3.73%
```

PC1 clearly separated the NM and MP46 groups, while biological replicates
clustered according to condition.

This indicates that the largest source of expression variation in the dataset
corresponds to the biological comparison.

## Sample-to-Sample Correlation

Pearson correlation was calculated between samples using transformed
expression values.

![](images/sample_correlation_heatmap.png){fig-alt="Sample-to-sample Pearson correlation heatmap" width=80%}

Within-group correlations were high:

```text
NM:       approximately 0.96
MP46:     approximately 0.96–0.98
```

Correlations between the two groups were lower:

```text
approximately 0.56–0.64
```

The agreement among biological replicates and the lower correlation between
groups were consistent with the PCA results.

Together, these independent expression-level QC analyses supported retaining
all six samples for differential-expression testing.

# Differential Expression

Differential-expression analysis was performed with **DESeq2**.

DESeq2 models RNA-seq counts using a negative-binomial statistical framework
while accounting for sequencing-depth differences and biological variability
among replicates.

The model was:

```text
Design:     ~ Group
Contrast:   MP46 vs NM
Reference:  NM
```

A positive log2 fold change therefore represents higher expression in MP46,
whereas a negative value represents higher expression in NM.

Significant differential expression was defined as:

```text
adjusted p-value < 0.05
AND
|log2FoldChange| ≥ log2(1.5)
```

The fold-change threshold corresponds to an expression difference of at least
**1.5-fold** in either direction.

## Differential-Expression Summary

| Result | Genes |
|---|---:|
| Genes tested | 12,728 |
| padj < 0.05 | 8,501 |
| Significant after padj + fold-change threshold | **6,816** |
| Higher in MP46 | **3,495** |
| Higher in NM | **3,321** |

GENCODE v48 annotations were added to the DESeq2 results to provide gene
symbols and gene types for biological interpretation.

## Volcano Plot

![](images/volcano_MP46_vs_NM.png){fig-alt="Volcano plot of MP46 versus NM differential expression" width=85%}

The volcano plot displays expression fold change against statistical
significance, highlighting genes with both substantial and statistically
supported differences between MP46 and NM.

## MA Plot

![](images/MA_MP46_vs_NM.png){fig-alt="MA plot for MP46 versus NM" width=85%}

The MA plot displays log2 fold change across the range of average gene
expression, providing a complementary view of expression differences and their
relationship to gene abundance.

## Differential-Expression Heatmap

![](images/top30_DE_heatmap.png){fig-alt="Heatmap of the top 30 differentially expressed genes" width=80%}

The heatmap shows the expression patterns of the top differentially expressed
genes across the six samples.

The clustering pattern provides a sample-level view of the transcriptional
differences identified by DESeq2.

# Functional Enrichment

Differential-expression analysis identifies individual genes, but biological
interpretation also requires understanding whether groups of genes participate
in related biological functions or pathways.

Significant genes were separated according to expression direction:

```text
Higher in MP46
Higher in NM
```

Functional enrichment was evaluated using:

- **Gene Ontology Biological Process (GO BP)**
- **Reactome pathways**

All genes tested by DESeq2 were used as the enrichment background.

## Enrichment Summary

| Gene set | GO BP | Reactome |
|---|---:|---:|
| Higher in MP46 | **31** | **0** |
| Higher in NM | **236** | **46** |

## Biological Processes Higher in MP46

![](images/GO_BP_Higher_in_MP46_summary.png){fig-alt="GO Biological Process enrichment for genes higher in MP46" width=90%}

Genes with higher expression in MP46 were primarily associated with biological
processes involving **cell division, microtubule organization,
centrosome-associated processes, and organelle fission**.

## Biological Processes Higher in NM

![](images/GO_BP_Higher_in_NM_summary.png){fig-alt="GO Biological Process enrichment for genes higher in NM" width=90%}

Genes with higher expression in NM showed broader enrichment involving
**extracellular matrix organization, cell adhesion, antigen processing, and
immune-related signaling**.

## Reactome Pathways Higher in NM

![](images/Reactome_Higher_in_NM_summary.png){fig-alt="Reactome pathway enrichment for genes higher in NM" width=90%}

Reactome analysis identified **46 significantly enriched pathways** among genes
with higher expression in NM.

No Reactome pathway passed the predefined significance threshold for genes
higher in MP46. The original threshold was retained rather than relaxed to
force pathway discovery.

# Integrated Interpretation

The individual analysis stages provide complementary evidence about the
dataset.

Raw-read QC indicated that the sequencing data were suitable for alignment
without additional trimming. STAR subsequently produced high unique mapping
rates across all samples.

Expression-level QC provided an independent check after gene quantification.
PCA showed clear separation between NM and MP46, while sample correlation
showed strong agreement among biological replicates.

DESeq2 identified **6,816 genes** meeting the predefined statistical and
fold-change thresholds, with 3,495 showing higher expression in MP46 and 3,321
showing higher expression in NM.

Functional enrichment then translated these gene-level differences into
broader biological patterns. Genes higher in MP46 were associated primarily
with cell-division-related processes, whereas genes higher in NM showed
enrichment for extracellular matrix, adhesion, antigen-processing, and
immune-related functions.

Together, the raw-read QC, alignment results, expression-level QC,
differential-expression analysis, and functional enrichment provide a
consistent view of substantial transcriptional differences between the two
groups.

These results describe associations within this dataset and do not by
themselves establish causal biological mechanisms.

# Reproducible Workflow

The analysis was first developed and validated as individual Python, R, and
command-line steps and then connected using **Nextflow DSL2**.

RNA-seq workflows contain many dependent processes and intermediate files.
Nextflow manages these dependencies automatically, tracks process inputs and
outputs, caches completed work, and allows interrupted or previously completed
analyses to continue using `-resume`.

The current Nextflow implementation **reuses the resulting STAR BAM files** and
automates the downstream analysis.

**Docker** provides controlled software environments for workflow processes,
reducing dependency on software installed directly on the host computer.

The project also demonstrates **Linux and SLURM** research-computing concepts,
including shared project storage, Environment Modules, resource requests, job
submission, and job monitoring.

These components serve complementary roles:

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| Git / GitHub | Version-controlled code and documentation |
| Docker | Reproducible software environments |
| Nextflow | Automated workflow execution |
| Linux / SLURM | Research-computing environment |
| Quarto | Reproducible and shareable reporting |

Together, they connect the biological analysis with the computational
practices needed to make the workflow reproducible and reviewable.

# Software

| Analysis component | Software |
|---|---|
| Raw-read QC | FastQC |
| QC aggregation | MultiQC 1.35 |
| Alignment | STAR |
| BAM processing | SAMtools |
| Strandedness assessment | RSeQC |
| Gene quantification | featureCounts |
| Count processing and visualization | Python |
| Differential expression | DESeq2 |
| Functional enrichment | clusterProfiler / ReactomePA |
| Gene annotation | GENCODE v48 |
| Workflow automation | Nextflow DSL2 |
| Containerization | Docker |
| Research computing | Linux / SLURM |
| Reporting | Quarto |
| Version control | Git / GitHub |

# Conclusion

This project demonstrates an end-to-end bulk RNA-seq analysis progressing from
raw paired-end sequencing reads to biological interpretation.

Raw-read QC was interpreted rather than treated as a simple PASS/FAIL
decision. MultiQC supported proceeding without unnecessary trimming, and
subsequent alignment, PCA, and sample-correlation analyses provided independent
checks of data and sample quality.

Differential-expression analysis identified substantial transcriptional
differences between MP46 and NM, while functional enrichment provided
biological context for those changes.

Nextflow automation, Docker environments, version-controlled analysis code,
Linux/SLURM computing practices, and Quarto reporting bring these individual
steps together into a reproducible and reviewable bioinformatics workflow.
